title: The Forest and the City: The Cultural Landscape of Urban Woodland, Second Edition
review_question: To analyze city forests as cultural and social landscapes, focusing on the many essential links that cities and their forests have had over time, and to understand how to strengthen and develop their social and cultural roles for creating better, more sustainable, and resilient urban areas in a rapidly changing world.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The book primarily focuses on cases from North-western and Northern Europe, but also includes examples from other parts of the world.

findings.consequent: Cultural landscapes, places, and spaces
findings.source: City Forests as Cultural Landscapes, Place, and Space (p. 11)
findings.quote: In this book, city forests are studied as cultural landscapes. ... From an experiential perspective, they can be both space and place.

findings.consequent: Antidote to the city and its hustle and bustle
findings.quote: forests have always provided a kind of antidote to the city and its hustle and bustle.

findings.consequent: Symbolic and spiritual meanings to people
findings.source: Ancient Spiritual Links Between Forests and People (p. 20)
findings.quote: Forests and trees have had symbolic and spiritual meanings to people for a long time.

findings.consequent: Places of worship
findings.quote: sacred groves emerged. The establishment and protection of groves have been a widespread tradition in many cultures.

findings.consequent: Natural, spiritual settings for churches, other places of worship and cemeteries
findings.quote: City forests provide natural, spiritual settings for churches, other places of worship and cemeteries.

findings.consequent: Inner peace, connectedness, reflection on the cycle of life and death, smallness in grand scheme of things
findings.quote: being in the woods was associated with inner peace, the experience of connectedness and reflections on the cycle of life and death and one’s smallness in the grand scheme of things.

findings.consequent: Spirituality, freedom, adventure
findings.quote: 'Wilder' nature plays a particularly important role in terms of spirituality, offering 'space' for freedom and adventure in contrast to safe 'place'.

findings.consequent: Stress-reducing and attention-restoring benefits, self-confidence, sense of belonging, renewed clarity
findings.quote: Wilderness experience has also been associated with a range of spiritual and transcendent values that can result in greater self-confidence, sense of belonging to something greater than oneself, and renewed clarity on ‘what really matters’.

findings.consequent: Places of fear and exclusion
findings.quote: Yet, like all forests, they also have a ‘darker’ side. Jones and Cloke (2002) mention that ‘places of trees’ can be places of fear as well as of exclusion.

findings.consequent: Mystery, danger (criminals, dangerous animals, mythical beings), getting lost
findings.quote: forests and woods have always been imbued with a certain degree of mystery. They have been believed... to be peopled with 'crowds of strange beings'.

findings.consequent: Feelings of containment and freedom
findings.quote: Woodlands often contain highly enclosed environments... paradoxically inspiring feelings of both containment and freedom.

findings.antecedent: Forests adjacent to population centres and transportation corridors
findings.consequent: Higher crime densities
findings.quote: crime densities do tend to be concentrated – perhaps not surprisingly – in forests adjacent to population centres and transportation corridors.

findings.antecedent: Lack of supervision and social control in urban woodlands
findings.consequent: Increased crime and vandalism
findings.quote: The cemetery had gradually deteriorated, attracting unwanted ‘uses’... and vandalism. ... lack of supervision and social control.

findings.antecedent: Higher densities of trees and better grass maintenance
findings.consequent: Increased sense of safety amongst residents
findings.quote: higher densities of trees and better grass maintenance contributed to an increased sense of safety amongst residents.

findings.consequent: Promoted self-esteem and sense of self
findings.quote: wilderness and outdoor challenge programmes for youths help promote their self-esteem and sense of self.

findings.consequent: Crucial source of products (timber, fuelwood, food, fodder, water)
findings.quote: Forests, including city forests, have always provided our society with a wide range of benefits, starting with meeting the dietary needs of humans and their farmed animals, as well as for fuelwood and construction materials.

findings.antecedent: Elite appropriation of city forests (hunting domains)
findings.consequent: Conservation of city forests
findings.source: From Wooded Commons to Elitist Prestige (p. 70)
findings.quote: The strong protective measures taken helped conserve several of these hunting domains until today.

findings.consequent: Property values
findings.quote: Nearby green space can have a significant effect on property values. People consider having green space nearby as an important argument for buying a house.

findings.consequent: Gentrification and higher house/rental prices
findings.quote: The greening of areas can lead to gentrification, and higher house and rental prices can push lower income residents out of the neighbourhood.

findings.consequent: Opportunities for escape and retreat from urban routines
findings.quote: City forests have always taken a rather special place within urban societies. On the one hand, they are an integral part of it, while on the other they offer – at least the illusion of – a possibility for escape and retreat.

findings.consequent: Popularity as recreational escapes
findings.quote: Recreational use of city forests increased further during the twentieth century. City forests started to attract thousands of visits per hectare annually.

findings.consequent: 'Window to the wider world', introducing people to plants, animals, people and cultures of other parts of the world
findings.quote: City forests do not only offer people with opportunities to recreate, they also provide a kind of ‘window to the wider world’.

findings.antecedent: Nature-based forms of recreation and tourism
findings.consequent: Increased rapidly
findings.quote: A trend towards more nature-based forms of recreation has also been noted... have increased rapidly, especially during recent years.

findings.consequent: Freedom and opportunity to escape from daily city life
findings.quote: City forests are appreciated as offering – at least to some extent – this ‘otherness’, and as providers of freedom and opportunity to escape from daily city life.

findings.consequent: Settings for art, inspiration for writers, poets, painters
findings.quote: City forests have played a special role in inspiring artists. These forests are situated close to the artistic centres that many cities and towns are.

findings.consequent: Strengthening ties between city forests and local inhabitants, enhancing place making and community building
findings.quote: In city forestry, art can help in enhancing linkages between forests, cities and communities. ... art can supply and reinforce sense of identity and loyalty to a place.

findings.consequent: High variety of species of plants and animals (biodiversity hotspots)
findings.quote: Various studies have confirmed that urban areas often harbour a perhaps surprisingly high variety of species of plants and animals.

findings.consequent: 'Real nature' close to where people live and work
findings.quote: Perhaps more importantly, to many city dwellers they also offer ‘real nature’ close to where they live and work.

findings.consequent: Reduced stress and improved mental ability
findings.source: City Forests, Mental Health and Well-Being (p. 136)
findings.quote: Contact with nature can have a powerful therapeutic or preventative effect on many people. ... contact with nature can reduce stress and help improve mental ability as well.

findings.consequent: Stronger positive health effect than urban landscapes
findings.source: City Forests, Mental Health and Well-Being (p. 136)
findings.quote: natural landscapes have a stronger positive health effect than urban landscapes. Most studies confirm this, but not much information is available about the magnitude of the differences.

findings.consequent: Reduced feelings of anger, frustration, aggression; enhanced social safety
findings.source: City Forests, Mental Health and Well-Being (p. 137)
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that exposure to natural environments may reduce feelings of anger, frustration, and aggression. In turn, this may enhance feelings of social safety.

findings.consequent: Improved physical health, longevity, reduced obesity and coronary heart diseases
findings.quote: That regular physical activity in nature improves people’s physical health has been shown in literature reviews by, among other, Jorgensen and Anthopoulou (2007) and WHO (2016).

findings.antecedent: Windows looking on forest scenery (for office workers)
findings.consequent: Lower levels of stress and higher job satisfaction
findings.quote: A study in South Korea indicated that office workers with windows looking on forest scenery have lower levels of stress and higher job satisfaction.

findings.consequent: Lower levels of (self-reported) stress
findings.quote: Nearness to green areas and (as a result) higher numbers of visits to green space are associated with lower levels of (self-reported) stress.

findings.consequent: Testing grounds for exotic tree species, new forestry approaches, environmental education
findings.quote: City forests have had various educational roles, and thus these forests can be considered as Forests of Learning. ... important testing grounds, for example for the introduction of exotic tree species as well as for the development of new approaches and methods in forestry.

findings.consequent: Mental and physical development, health, learning, creativity, social bonding, understanding of nature
findings.quote: growing body of research that shows the importance of children spending time in nature, for example for their mental and physical development, health, learning, creativity, social bonding, and understanding of nature and natural processes.

findings.antecedent: Children's active free-play in wild environments
findings.consequent: Personal development, social and community skills
findings.source: Forests as Settings for Play and Adventure (p. 159, 163)
findings.quote: The wild environment can play an important role in meeting the development needs of young people. ... strengthens the personal development, as well as social and community skills of youths.

findings.consequent: Bringing children outdoors, increased exercise, family bonding
findings.source: Forests as Settings for Play and Adventure (p. 161)
findings.quote: The game did attract both children and their parents, and thus results in joint gaming outside. ... including increased exercise, more time spent outdoors and opportunities for family bonding.

findings.consequent: Positive impact on children's confidence, social skills, language, communication, motivation, concentration, physical skills, knowledge, understanding
findings.quote: Forest schools in England and Wales offer many benefits, such as a positive impact on children in terms of confidence, social skills, language and communication, motivation and concentration, physical skills and knowledge and understanding.

findings.consequent: Development, identity, cohesion of local urban communities
findings.quote: This chapter highlights another important role of these forests, namely the contributions these forests (can) make to the development, identity and cohesion of local urban communities.

findings.consequent: Social equity and political participation
findings.quote: Public access to city forests is crucial in realising the place making potential of city forests and trees... even be regarded a cornerstone of democracy and social equity.

findings.antecedent: Community involvement in planning and management of city forests
findings.consequent: Strengthened community bonds and trust
findings.quote: Public involvement can help, for example, in developing mutual understanding between decision-makers, city foresters and residents.

findings.consequent: Ecosystems more resilient to climate change, pests, diseases
findings.quote: high biodiversity resulting in ecosystems that are more resilient to climate change, pests and diseases, and other pressures, while also providing a wider range of ecosystem services.

findings.antecedent: Increasing migration and growing diversity in urban populations
findings.consequent: Diverse views, demands, and needs for urban nature
findings.source: Growing Diversity in Forest Users, Uses and Preferences (p. 189)
findings.quote: Different urban dwellers have different views, demands, and needs when it comes to urban forests, and urban nature in general. These views, demands and needs are becoming even more diverse with the changing composition of our urban populations.
key_citations: Jensen and Andersen, Peters and Andersen (2013)

findings.consequent: Hampered planning and management, obstacles for future forests
findings.quote: city forest conflicts can hamper planning and management, and act as important obstacles for realising the city Forests for the Future.

findings.consequent: Sign of people's commitment to 'their' city forests
findings.quote: On the other hand, conflicts are a sign of people’s commitment to ‘their’ city forests.

synthesis_conclusions: City forests have a long and rich tradition, providing cultural, social, economic, and environmental benefits to urban communities.
City forests are appreciated for contributing to a pleasant living, working, and leisure environment, offering learning opportunities, fostering local pride, and connecting people to nature.
City forests have been at the forefront of re-appreciating the important role of forests and nature in urbanized societies.
City forestry and related approaches are crucial for the future evolution of what is considered a 'forest' in urban contexts.
City forests can significantly contribute to creating better cities by forming attractive, multifunctional urban landscapes.
The heritage of individual city forests should be cherished, recognizing their unique landscapes and the diverse social and cultural roles they have played.
Forestry, particularly in urban settings, is increasingly influenced by urban societies' values and demands, requiring adaptation to these perceptions and needs.
City forests represent a true symbiosis of nature and people, essential for the future of urban environments.
evidence_gaps: Lack of exploration on how increasing diversity of spiritual beliefs affects city forest management and how spirituality can be incorporated into planning processes in multicultural communities.
Limited knowledge about outdoor recreation habits of non-Western immigrants in Europe, with study results being difficult to compare due to differing methods and ethnic affiliation categories.
Insufficient knowledge about the impact of increasing human diversity on how urban forests are used and shaped, and its role in inclusive decision-making and planning.
Lack of scientific evidence on health effects and mechanisms of outdoor environments (including forests) on public health, hindering widespread use for health promotion.
Economic aspects: green space is often seen as a luxury rather than a necessity in urban areas, despite growing evidence of health benefits.
Need for more knowledge on causal relationships and mechanisms between forest/nature use, views, and health/well-being, and which types of landscapes have most positive effects.
Very few studies have corroborated findings on the relationship between tree density/maintenance and perceived safety in urban green spaces.
Community participation in city forest management is often local and short-term, lacking strategic long-term approaches.
Insufficient attention given to visual aspects and design of new urban woodlands.
The 'real adventure' potential of city forests, including a more pleasant perspective on the Forest of Fear, remains to be fully developed.
heterogeneity_sources: Differing methods and categories used in studies on ethnic affiliation and nature perception, making results difficult to compare.

moderators.effect: Elderly people (over 65 years) in Britain do not seem to be more afraid of crime than other urban woodland users, but have specific fears related to old age (e.g., stumbling and falling).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Elderly vs. other urban woodland users

moderators.effect: Women are often afraid to go into forests by themselves, fearing for personal safety and sexual assault. They require larger groups to feel safe compared to men.

Different urban dwellers have varying views, demands, and needs for urban forests and nature. Some immigrants of non-Western backgrounds are less appreciative of wilderness areas or afraid to visit forests, may lack information, or feel unwelcome.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Dutch descent vs. new immigrants; British, Chinese, Italian, Portuguese descent; Caribbean Latinos; Asian and Afro-Caribbean women

moderators.effect: Lower income groups and retired people primarily use inner-city public green, while most of the population seeks recreation in surrounding hills/natural areas. Poorer residents often lack resources to enhance urban forest on their property.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Lower income vs. higher income groups

moderators.effect: Distance to the forest is an important factor for its use. Most city forests are particularly used by local people living within easy walking/cycling distance (300-500m).

limitations: The book has a bias towards North-western and Northern Europe, as these parts of the world are most familiar to the author, potentially limiting the generalizability of some insights.
